secondaryCondition: L5/S1 lumbosacral radiculopathy with sciatic-distribution impairment
secondaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.124a, DC 8520 (sciatic nerve); DC 8620 for neuritis or 8720 for neuralgia when that phenotype is the appropriate rating basis
primaryCondition: Service-connected lumbar degenerative disc disease with a clinically concordant herniation or foraminal/lateral-recess stenosis
primaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.71a, DC 5242 for degenerative disc disease other than intervertebral disc syndrome; DC 5243 only when disc herniation compresses and/or irritates the adjacent nerve root
etiologicalMechanism:
Anatomical causal sequence: lumbar disc degeneration and a concordant herniation or stenotic lesion can compromise a spinal nerve root in the lateral recess, neural foramen, or extraforaminal region. A paracentral L4-L5 herniation commonly affects the traversing L5 root, whereas a paracentral L5-S1 herniation commonly affects S1; a foraminal lesion can affect the exiting root instead. Root dysfunction may produce radiating neuropathic pain, sensory change, myotomal weakness, and reflex abnormalities. These are nerve-root findings, not proof of a distal sciatic-nerve lesion; the sciatic rating family is selected for the resulting functional distribution. Berry et al. (PMID 31788391) describes compression by disc bulging/herniation and degenerative narrowing, clinical localization, MRI, and electrodiagnostic differentiation. The NASS guideline (PMID 24239490) provides a systematic-review-based diagnostic and management framework for symptomatic lumbar disc herniation with radiculopathy. Mechanical compression is the central established pathway. A secondary chemical contribution from exposed disc material and local inflammatory mediators is plausible, but Goupille et al. (PMID 9726337) explicitly states that the role of the identified mediators in producing human radicular pain was not proven and may be transient. Do not convert that mechanistic hypothesis into a proven TNF-alpha-mediated cause in an individual claim.

Required individual evidence: identify the service-connected lumbar segment and review dated pre-onset records, the side and root distribution of symptoms, motor and sensory examination, reflexes, and an anatomically concordant MRI or CT myelogram. EMG/nerve-conduction testing can help when imaging and symptoms disagree or a peripheral neuropathy is suspected; it is not an obligatory positive test in every clinical radiculopathy and can be nondiagnostic in sensory-predominant disease. Incidental disc degeneration, axial back pain alone, and nonspecific leg pain do not establish this relationship. Competing causes include diabetic or other length-dependent neuropathy, common-peroneal entrapment, plexopathy, hip disease, vascular claudication, and a separate nonservice-connected spinal lesion. A selective root-block response can corroborate localization but is not independently dispositive. New bladder dysfunction, saddle sensory loss, or rapidly progressive weakness requires urgent assessment rather than routine nexus processing.

Legal theory: this is secondary causation under 38 CFR § 3.310(a) when the service-connected disc lesion produces the documented radiculopathy; it is not a medication side effect. If a separate radiculopathy already existed and the service-connected lesion increased its severity, analyze aggravation under § 3.310(b) separately, documenting the prior baseline, attributable increment, and natural progression. An examiner may conclude that the relationship is 'at least as likely as not' only after explaining why the veteran's anatomical concordance, chronology, and competing-cause assessment place the positive and negative evidence at least in approximate balance. No individual probability is asserted by this population-level mapping.

Rating and graph controls: § 4.71a's General Rating Formula Note (1) directs separate evaluation of associated objective neurologic abnormalities under the appropriate code; § 4.14 prohibits counting the same manifestation twice. DC 5243's incapacitating-episode method is an alternative to the combined General Formula approach, not an automatic extra award, and requires physician-prescribed bed rest. Select sciatic versus femoral or other nerve codes from documented function rather than coding every lumbar root as sciatic. The repository already has degenerative-disc-disease → radiculopathy; this anatomically scoped radiculopathy-sciatic proposal must be reconciled with that generic edge, not added as a duplicate recommendation.

medicalEvidence.title: A Review of Lumbar Radiculopathy, Diagnosis, and Treatment
medicalEvidence.authors: James A Berry; Christopher Elia; Harneel S Saini; Dan E Miulli
medicalEvidence.summary: Clinical review describing degenerative and disc-related nerve-root compression, dermatomal/myotomal examination, MRI, and the role and limitations of electrodiagnostic testing. Supports the anatomical pathway and diagnostic safeguards; it does not establish a veteran-specific nexus or an individual probability.

medicalEvidence.title: An evidence-based clinical guideline for the diagnosis and treatment of lumbar disc herniation with radiculopathy
medicalEvidence.authors: D Scott Kreiner; Steven W Hwang; John E Easa; et al.; North American Spine Society
medicalEvidence.summary: NASS systematic review and evidence-based guideline addressing 29 clinical questions using graded evidence and explicitly identified consensus statements. Provides a clinical standard for diagnosing and treating symptomatic disc herniation with radiculopathy, not proof that incidental degeneration explains every leg complaint.

medicalEvidence.title: The role of inflammation in disk herniation-associated radiculopathy
medicalEvidence.authors: P Goupille; M I Jayson; J P Valat; A J Freemont
medicalEvidence.summary: Review identifies inflammatory mediators in herniated disc material but expressly concludes that their role in radiculopathy was not proven and that inflammation may be transient. Included as a mechanistic limitation: biochemical plausibility supplements, rather than replaces, anatomical and clinical evidence.

cfrCitations: 38 CFR § 4.71a, DC 5242 and DC 5243; General Rating Formula, Note (1)

secondaryCondition: Cervical radiculopathy affecting an upper-extremity radicular group
secondaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.124a, DC 8510 (upper radicular group), 8511 (middle), 8512 (lower), or 8513 (all groups), selected by documented distribution; corresponding 8610-8613 neuritis or 8710-8713 neuralgia codes when appropriate
primaryCondition: Service-connected cervical degenerative disc disease with disc herniation or spondylotic foraminal stenosis
primaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.71a, DC 5242; DC 5243 only for disc herniation with compression and/or irritation of the adjacent nerve root; DC 5238 when spinal stenosis is the diagnosed rating basis
etiologicalMechanism:
Anatomical causal sequence: a cervical disc herniation can impinge the adjacent nerve root, while degenerative loss of disc height and uncinate/facet hypertrophy can narrow the neural foramen even without a large soft-disc extrusion. Iyer and Kim (PMID 27250042; full text PMC4958381) describes disc-height loss, increased loading of the intervertebral joints, bony hypertrophy, foraminal narrowing, and nerve-root compression. Compression can disturb local perfusion and neural conduction, with local inflammatory sensitization contributing to pain; neither cytokine levels nor a specific biochemical cascade must be demonstrated in order to diagnose a clinically concordant compressive radiculopathy. Caridi et al. (PMID 23024624) identifies spondylosis and disc herniation as common causes and describes dermatomal pain/paresthesias with possible weakness. Abbed and Coumans (PMID 17204882) specifically identifies cervical disc herniation and spondylosis as frequent causes of root compression and inflammation.

Localization matters: C5-C6 pathology commonly affects C6, C6-C7 affects C7, and C7-T1 affects C8. The examiner should map pain, sensory findings, myotomal weakness, and reflexes against the actual lesion and side; for example, C6 may involve the radial forearm/thumb with biceps or wrist-extension weakness, whereas C7 may involve the middle finger and triceps. These clinical root distributions guide examination but do not automatically dictate one VA radicular-group code. MRI must be interpreted with the examination because common age-related degenerative findings can be incidental. CT may better define bony stenosis, and EMG/nerve-conduction studies can help distinguish root disease from distal entrapment when needed. A normal or nondiagnostic EMG does not by itself exclude radiculopathy. Progressive motor deficits, gait change, hyperreflexia, or other myelopathic signs require timely spine evaluation; myelopathy is not interchangeable with an isolated radiculopathy.

Competing explanations include median or ulnar entrapment, shoulder pathology, brachial plexopathy/Parsonage-Turner syndrome, generalized neuropathy, and neoplasm or another independent spinal process. Coexisting distal entrapment and root disease may both be present; a 'double-crush' label cannot substitute for identifying each lesion. Neck pain alone or hand tingling without root concordance is insufficient. Surgical decompression or targeted-treatment response can corroborate but does not independently prove the origin or service connection of the cervical disease.

Legal theory: secondary causation under 38 CFR § 3.310(a), provided the cervical pathology is itself service connected or supported through a separately established chain. Service-connected lumbar degeneration does not automatically establish service connection for cervical degeneration. If cervical disease worsens a pre-existing nonservice-connected root disorder instead of originating it, address § 3.310(b) aggravation independently with baseline findings and an attributable increase beyond natural progression. An 'at least as likely as not' opinion must integrate a compatible timeline, lesion-to-root concordance, and competing causes; neither radiographic prevalence nor the general causal mechanism establishes the probability in an individual veteran.

Rating and graph controls: evaluate objective neurologic abnormalities separately under § 4.71a Note (1) when warranted, record affected side and dominant versus nondominant arm, and apply § 4.14 to avoid rating the same weakness or sensory deficit under overlapping group and distal-nerve codes. Use DC 8513 only when all radicular groups are actually involved, not as a default. Project to radiculopathy-upper-extremity; reconcile this specific identity with the existing generic degenerative-disc-disease → radiculopathy edge before authoring.

medicalEvidence.title: Cervical radiculopathy
medicalEvidence.summary: Review covers disc herniation and spondylotic foraminal narrowing, root-localizing clinical findings, MRI/CT, electrodiagnostic limitations, natural history, and management. Its full text explicitly describes disc-height loss and uncinate hypertrophy as mechanisms of foraminal stenosis. Does not establish causation from an incidental scan alone.

medicalEvidence.title: Cervical radiculopathy: a review
medicalEvidence.authors: John M Caridi; Matthias Pumberger; Alexander P Hughes
medicalEvidence.summary: Clinical review identifies facet spondylosis and intervertebral disc herniation as common causes of cervical nerve-root compression and links the syndrome to dermatomal pain/paresthesias and possible weakness. Supports clinical, imaging, and electrophysiologic correlation rather than automatic inference from degeneration.

medicalEvidence.title: Cervical radiculopathy: pathophysiology, presentation, and clinical evaluation
medicalEvidence.authors: Khalid M Abbed; Jean-Valéry C E Coumans
medicalEvidence.summary: Review describes compression and inflammation of cervical roots in the neural foramen, frequently from cervical disc herniation or spondylosis, and warns that entrapment neuropathies can mimic or coexist with the syndrome. Supports the causal anatomy and differential-diagnosis requirements.

cfrCitations: 38 CFR § 4.71a, DC 5238, DC 5242, DC 5243; General Rating Formula, Note (1)

primaryCondition: Service-connected gastroesophageal reflux disease with chronic reflux esophagitis
etiologicalMechanism:
Injury-repair causal sequence: repeated reflux exposure can cause esophagitis and ulcerative injury; healing of sustained injury can produce fibrotic scar and a fixed luminal narrowing, usually distal in a peptic stricture. The resulting mechanical resistance to bolus passage causes dysphagia and may require repeated dilation. This is a GERD → reflux esophagitis → peptic stricture pathway, not a claim that every episode of heartburn causes irreversible fibrosis. Pregun et al. (PMID 19439958) identifies peptic stricture as a consequence of GERD, emphasizes exclusion of malignancy, and explains why healing coexistent esophagitis and effective acid suppression reduce repeated dilation. In the 366-patient randomized trial by Smith et al. (PMID 7926495), omeprazole versus ranitidine after dilation reduced the proportion needing redilation at 12 months from 46% to 30% among the reported evaluable groups. This intervention evidence supports an ongoing acid-dependent contribution to recurrence; it does not prove the cause of all benign strictures or estimate an individual nexus probability. The ACG guideline (PMID 34807007) supplies an evidence-based GERD evaluation and management standard.

Required individual evidence: establish documented GERD before the fibrotic lesion, retrieve serial endoscopy reports with stricture location, caliber and associated erosive findings, obtain biopsies as clinically indicated to exclude cancer and eosinophilic disease, and review barium imaging, dilation history, reflux-treatment history, and symptoms. A prior clinical diagnosis of GERD without objective or persuasive longitudinal support is not enough to label a new narrowing 'peptic.' Competing causes in the differential include esophageal malignancy, eosinophilic esophagitis, caustic ingestion, radiation injury, anastomotic narrowing, and pill-induced injury. Achalasia and other motility disorders can cause dysphagia without a peptic fixed narrowing. A short distal scar with prior erosive reflux and an appropriate treatment history supports the route, whereas a proximal or multifocal lesion, eosinophilic histology, cancer, or a relevant alternative exposure may favor a different etiology.

Legal theory: when service-connected GERD produces the documented peptic stricture, the connection is causation under 38 CFR § 3.310(a), not a medication side effect. If an independently caused stricture predates GERD, any reflux-related increase in recurrent narrowing or dysphagia belongs to an independently reasoned § 3.310(b) aggravation analysis. Record baseline caliber, dilation frequency, diet tolerance, and clinical severity from pre-aggravation or qualifying earliest records, and distinguish natural progression of the original lesion. An 'at least as likely as not' conclusion requires the veteran-specific temporal, endoscopic, histologic, and differential evidence to be at least approximately balanced; population evidence and treatment response alone cannot supply that conclusion.

Rating and graph controls: current DC 7203 requires documented stricture findings and grades dysphagia/treatment burden; DC 7206 also uses stricture-related criteria. Establishing a distinct diagnosis does not automatically permit two ratings for the same dysphagia, dilation burden, or nutritional impairment under § 4.14. Claim-period-specific criteria must be checked rather than applying obsolete GERD-by-hiatal-hernia coding to every claim. The repository already carries esophagitis → esophageal-stricture → dysphagia. Preserve that intermediate-node physiology and perform a redundancy review before adding a direct GERD → stricture shortcut; source PMID 19439958 is already registered and requires provenance-aware reuse rather than a duplicate source entity.

medicalEvidence.title: Peptic esophageal stricture: medical treatment
medicalEvidence.authors: István Pregun; István Hritz; Zsolt Tulassay; László Herszényi
medicalEvidence.summary: Review identifies peptic stricture as a consequence of GERD, requires diagnostic exclusion of malignancy, and describes acid suppression, dilation and surgery. Healing coexistent esophagitis is important to outcome; proton-pump inhibitors can reduce repeated dilation. The route is scoped to confirmed peptic strictures, not all dysphagia.

medicalEvidence.title: A comparison of omeprazole and ranitidine in the prevention of recurrence of benign esophageal stricture. Restore Investigator Group
medicalEvidence.authors: P M Smith; G D Kerr; R Cockel; B A Ross; C M Bate; P Brown; M W Dronfield; J R Green; W S Hislop; A Theodossi
medicalEvidence.summary: Double-blind randomized trial enrolled 366 patients after dilation. At 12 months, redilation was needed in 43/143 (30%) on omeprazole versus 66/143 (46%) on ranitidine, P<0.01. Supports acid suppression reducing recurrence in the studied population, not automatic veteran-specific causation or a present-day recommendation to use ranitidine.

medicalEvidence.title: ACG Clinical Guideline for the Diagnosis and Management of Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease
medicalEvidence.authors: Philip O Katz; Kerry B Dunbar; Felice H Schnoll-Sussman; Katarina B Greer; Rena Yadlapati; Stuart Jon Spechler
medicalEvidence.summary: GRADE-based clinical guideline provides evidence-based evaluation and management of GERD, including pharmacologic, lifestyle, endoscopic, and surgical approaches. Supports appropriate confirmation and management of the upstream disease; it is a clinical standard, not a stricture-specific causation trial.

secondaryCondition: Drug-induced parkinsonism from dopamine-receptor-blocking antipsychotic exposure
secondaryDiagnosticCode: No dedicated drug-induced-parkinsonism DC is listed. 38 CFR §§ 4.20 and 4.27 permit a clinically justified analogous code; DC 8004 (paralysis agitans) under § 4.124a is a candidate analogy only, not an automatic diagnosis or award; qualified-human rating review required
primaryCondition: Service-connected schizophrenia treated with a dopamine-receptor-blocking antipsychotic
primaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.130, DC 9201 (schizophrenia); DC 9203 is removed and must not be substituted
etiologicalMechanism:
Pharmacological causal sequence: an antipsychotic prescribed for service-connected schizophrenia can block postsynaptic striatal D2 receptors. In the basal-ganglia motor circuit, D2 blockade disinhibits the indirect-pathway striatal output, increasing downstream inhibitory output to thalamocortical motor systems and producing bradykinesia and rigidity, with tremor or impaired gait in some patients. Shin and Chung (PMID 22523509; full text PMC3325428) describes this circuit and distinguishes postsynaptic blockade from the presynaptic nigrostriatal degeneration typical of idiopathic Parkinson disease. The proximate exposure is the documented medication, not schizophrenia itself. Feldman et al. (PMID 36573102) reviews culprit drugs, differential diagnosis, and management. Ali et al. (PMID 34506552) supplies a systematic review/meta-analysis of observational studies, with pooled antipsychotic-induced parkinsonism prevalence of 20% (95% CI 11-28%). That pooled prevalence quantifies a recognized adverse effect across heterogeneous exposed populations; it is neither a 20% probability that a particular veteran's syndrome is drug-caused nor proof of permanent neurodegeneration.

Required individual evidence: identify the exact antipsychotic, indication, starting date, dose changes, adherence, and concurrent dopamine-blocking medications. Compare dated baseline neurologic findings with the onset of bradykinesia, rigidity, tremor and functional impairment. A compatible onset after initiation or dose escalation and improvement after a clinician-supervised reduction or substitution support attribution, but deliberate rechallenge is not required and medication changes must be coordinated with psychiatry to avoid relapse. Persistence after withdrawal does not exclude a drug contribution; it can reflect prolonged drug effects or unmasking of underlying neurodegenerative disease. Symmetry alone is not diagnostic because drug-induced cases can be asymmetric. Neurologic review should distinguish competing causes, including idiopathic Parkinson disease, vascular parkinsonism, essential tremor, depressive/psychotic psychomotor slowing, tardive dyskinesia, akathisia, and other toxidromes. DAT imaging, when clinically appropriate, may help distinguish presynaptic degeneration from pure postsynaptic blockade but is not a universal required test. Do not relabel tardive dyskinesia, neuroleptic malignant syndrome, or serotonin syndrome as this identity.

Legal theory: 'Medication Side Effect' is the requested packet label. In 38 CFR § 3.310(a) it is a treatment-mediated secondary-causation theory: service-connected schizophrenia → medically documented antipsychotic exposure → drug-induced parkinsonism. It is not a fourth repository nexusClassification enum arm, and no negligence allegation is necessary to describe this secondary-service-connection mechanism. If a pre-existing Parkinson syndrome was instead worsened by necessary antipsychotic treatment, evaluate § 3.310(b) aggravation with a documented baseline and an attributable increase beyond its natural course; do not assert that the drug created the underlying neurodegenerative disease. An 'at least as likely as not' opinion needs the actual exposure chronology, movement-disorder examination, medication response where safely observed, and reasoned consideration of alternatives. No patient-specific probability is asserted here.

Rating and governance controls: schizophrenia uses current DC 9201. Drug-induced parkinsonism has no dedicated code; DC 8004 is identified only as an analogous-rating candidate requiring review of affected function, anatomical localization and symptomatology under §§ 4.20 and 4.27. Do not apply its minimum rating automatically, equate this syndrome with idiopathic Parkinson disease, or duplicate the same manifestations under § 4.14. The repository's batch-95 deferral and ME-29 held-evidence adjudication remain active. This newly located independent systematic-review anchor is presented for human reassessment, not an automatic lifting of that hold; reserved PMIDs 30695288 and 34652577 are not reused in this proposal.

medicalEvidence.title: Drug-induced parkinsonism
medicalEvidence.summary: Review explains basal-ganglia motor-circuit effects of dopamine-receptor blockade, culprit drugs, clinical overlap with Parkinson disease, and DAT imaging. Notes that asymmetry can occur and deficits may persist after stopping the drug. Supports treatment causation while rejecting an automatic equation with neurodegeneration.

medicalEvidence.title: Updated Perspectives on the Management of Drug-Induced Parkinsonism (DIP): Insights from the Clinic
medicalEvidence.authors: Matthew Feldman; Sarah Marmol; Jason Margolesky
medicalEvidence.summary: Clinical review differentiates secondary/iatrogenic parkinsonism from idiopathic Parkinson disease, describes motor and nonmotor diagnostic clues, identifies culprit medications, and discusses management. Supports individualized exposure and differential assessment rather than diagnosis from an antipsychotic prescription alone.

medicalEvidence.title: Antipsychotic-induced extrapyramidal side effects: A systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies
medicalEvidence.authors: Tilahun Ali; Mekonnen Sisay; Mandaras Tariku; Abraham Nigussie Mekuria; Assefa Desalew
medicalEvidence.summary: Systematic review/meta-analysis included 15 original articles and reported pooled antipsychotic-induced parkinsonism prevalence of 20% (95% CI 11-28%). Provides a non-case-report anchor for adverse-effect burden. Heterogeneous observational prevalence does not establish individual causality or satisfy a VA probability threshold by itself.

secondaryCondition: Pre-existing restless legs syndrome worsened in advanced chronic kidney disease
secondaryDiagnosticCode: No dedicated restless-legs-syndrome DC is listed. 38 CFR §§ 4.20 and 4.27 require an appropriate analogous rating; DC 8103 (convulsive tic) under § 4.124a is a possible comparator only when functions and symptomatology are sufficiently analogous, not a diagnosis of a tic disorder or an automatic rating
primaryCondition: Service-connected advanced chronic kidney disease requiring regular dialysis
primaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.115b, DC 7530 (chronic renal disease requiring regular dialysis), evaluated as renal dysfunction under § 4.115a; use the actual etiology-specific renal code if regular dialysis is not present
etiologicalMechanism:
Scope and proposed mechanism: this mapping addresses documented restless legs syndrome (RLS) that existed before advanced service-connected kidney disease and subsequently became more severe. It does not infer de novo causation from the fact that kidney disease and RLS coexist. The characteristic syndrome is an urge to move the legs with unpleasant sensations, provoked by rest, relieved by movement, and worse in the evening/night, after excluding mimics. Uremic illness and disordered iron availability can contribute to the sensorimotor syndrome in a susceptible person, but a single established biochemical cascade from reduced filtration to RLS has not been demonstrated. Brain-iron regulation, genetic susceptibility and altered neurotransmission are implicated in RLS generally; renal anemia is not interchangeable with proven brain-iron deficiency. Safarpour et al. (PMID 37008995) reports that most dialysis studies found RLS prevalence of 15-30% versus 5-10% in the general population, while correlations with iron, ferritin, electrolytes and parathyroid hormone were inconsistent. Trenkwalder et al. (PMID 26944272) specifically warns that the labels 'primary' and 'secondary' RLS can suggest an inappropriate causal relation and describes a genetic-environmental spectrum. Those cautions must remain in the mapping.

Clinical-standard anchor: the current AASM guideline (PMID 39324694; full text PMC11701286) recognizes an end-stage-renal-disease subgroup, recommends regular ferritin/transferrin-saturation assessment in clinically significant RLS, and conditionally supports IV iron sucrose in the ESRD subgroup with ferritin <200 ng/mL and transferrin saturation <20%. A treatment recommendation and clinical improvement after iron replacement support a modifiable contributor in selected patients, not proof that every case is caused by kidney disease. The guideline also stresses untreated sleep apnea and serotonergic, antihistaminergic, or antidopaminergic medications as exacerbating factors and cautions against standard long-term dopamine-agonist use because of augmentation. Do not repeat the older review's description of gabapentin/pregabalin as calcium-channel blockers: they are alpha2-delta ligands. No medication or iron dosing is prescribed by this mapping.

Required individual evidence: establish RLS with clinical criteria rather than diagnosing it from periodic movements on a sleep study alone; retrieve baseline symptom frequency, duration, onset time, sleep/function impact, treatment requirements and, where available, International RLS Severity Scale scores. Align subsequent worsening with renal progression/dialysis history, iron studies and medication changes. Distinguish actual RLS from dialysis-associated cramps, uremic neuropathy, positional discomfort, edema and akathisia. Assess nonrenal iron loss, longstanding familial RLS, pregnancy where relevant, untreated sleep apnea, caffeine/alcohol exposure, antidepressant or dopamine-blocker effects, and dopamine-agonist augmentation as alternate causes of the increased burden. Kidney severity or a high population prevalence alone is insufficient.

Legal theory: 38 CFR § 3.310(b) applies only to an attributable increase beyond the pre-existing RLS course and natural progression. Baseline must be supported by evidence predating aggravation or the qualifying earliest evidence between onset of aggravation and evidence of current severity; the rating activity determines baseline/current severity and the compensable increment. An examiner should separately address whether the worsening is 'at least as likely as not' due to service-connected CKD, using chronology, repeated clinical assessments, documented renal/iron changes, and comparison with competing explanations. Do not require permanent worsening as an added threshold, but do identify an actual attributable increase rather than diagnostic overlap. Without these individual data, the appropriate conclusion is that aggravation is a medically plausible, evidence-supported proposal, not an established patient nexus; the schema probability remains NOT_ASSERTED. If RLS began only after CKD, a separate causation analysis under § 3.310(a) is needed rather than inventing a pre-existing baseline.

Rating and graph controls: DC 7530 is specific to regular dialysis, not a universal CKD code. RLS is unlisted; the potential DC 8103 analogy requires qualified review rather than asserting that RLS is a convulsive tic. Avoid duplicating the same sleep or leg manifestations under § 4.14. Project to restless-leg-syndrome with an AGGRAVATION arm only if baselineProgression and aggravatingFactor are separately authored and clinically supportable; absent that evidence, retain association-only status instead of forcing this proposal into an established causal edge.

medicalEvidence.title: Restless Legs Syndrome in Chronic Kidney Disease- a Systematic Review
medicalEvidence.authors: Yasaman Safarpour; Nosratola D Vaziri; Bahman Jabbari
medicalEvidence.summary: Review found 175 articles and examined 111 clinical-trial/cross-sectional reports; most dialysis studies reported RLS prevalence of 15-30% compared with 5-10% in the general population. Correlations with iron/ferritin and other laboratory factors were inconsistent. Supports the renal-disease association and possible contributors, not universal causation or individual aggravation.

medicalEvidence.title: Restless legs syndrome associated with major diseases: A systematic review and new concept
medicalEvidence.authors: Claudia Trenkwalder; Richard Allen; Birgit Högl; Walter Paulus; Juliane Winkelmann
medicalEvidence.summary: Systematic review identifies increased RLS prevalence in iron deficiency and kidney disease but cautions that primary/secondary labels can imply an inappropriate causal relationship. Describes overlapping genetic and environmental contributions and potential reduction of symptoms after treating underlying disease. Included as an explicit limit on causal and aggravation inference.

medicalEvidence.title: Treatment of restless legs syndrome and periodic limb movement disorder: an American Academy of Sleep Medicine clinical practice guideline
medicalEvidence.authors: John W Winkelman; J Andrew Berkowski; Lourdes M DelRosso; Brian B Koo; Matthew T Scharf; Denise Sharon; Rochelle S Zak; Uzma Kazmi; Yngve Falck-Ytter; Anita V Shelgikar; Lynn Marie Trotti; Arthur S Walters
medicalEvidence.summary: GRADE-based guideline gives iron-assessment and exacerbating-factor guidance and ESRD-specific conditional recommendations, including IV iron sucrose for ferritin <200 ng/mL with transferrin saturation <20%. Highlights mimics and dopamine-agonist augmentation. These are clinical care standards; they do not establish a veteran's CKD-attributable aggravation without baseline and longitudinal evidence.

cfrCitations: 38 CFR § 3.310(a) (separate analysis if onset is new rather than pre-existing)
